## Slide 2 · Goals for today

Four goals today. You understand what Quarto is and how it relates to R Markdown
and knitr. You write your first Quarto document. You render Quarto documents into
html and PDF format. And you become aware of the specific challenges for project
management that arise when using Quarto — that last one connects directly back to
the session on R projects and the `here` package.

The session is structured in four parts: what Quarto is, Quarto step by step,
notes on project management, and avoiding common Quarto mistakes.

## Slide 4 · First: what is R Markdown?

Before we get to Quarto itself, a word on R Markdown, because Quarto grew out of
it.

R Markdown is a document format that allows you to write documents containing
code of two languages. R code to perform statistical analysis — which we know
almost completely by now. And Markdown code to create formatted text using a
plain text editor.

Markdown is readable in its source and, if rendered, allows for formatting such
as bold or italic fonts, tables, headings and so on. The left side shows the
source, the right side the rendered result.

Together, R and Markdown allow you to write formatted text and conduct
statistical analysis within one single file — which is perfect for making
research accessible and reproducible.

## Slide 5 · We skip the Markdown basics

We will not cover the basics of markdown here, because going through syntax rules
in a group is quite boring and you learn it far faster by doing.

Please do the interactive Markdown tutorial on the course webpage instead. It
takes about twenty minutes and it covers emphasis, paragraphs, headings,
blockquotes, lists, links, images, code and nested lists — everything you need.

## Slide 6 · And what about Quarto?

Quarto is basically a next-generation version of R Markdown.

It allows you to do everything you can do in R Markdown, but it works with more
languages, including Python and Julia, and it has a number of additional features
and capabilities.

R Markdown will stay around — a lot of existing material is written in it — but
there is no need for you to learn it any more. Everything we do from here on is
Quarto.

## Slide 7 · What is Quarto? The anatomy of a document

Here is a complete Quarto document on the left and what it renders to on the
right.

Four kinds of element. At the top, framed in blue, the header — it contains the
meta information. In orange, the markdown: the prose, the headings, the text
between the code. In red, the chunk options, which control how a given piece of
code behaves. And in green, the R chunks, which contain the actual code.

Note what happens on the right: the code produced a figure, the headings became
numbered sections, and a table of contents appeared — all of that came from the
header. We will go through each of these elements in turn.

## Slide 8 · One source, many output formats

Quarto documents can be rendered to very different formats, and it is worth
understanding the route they take.

Your qmd file goes to knitr, which executes the code and produces a plain
markdown file. That markdown file goes to pandoc, which converts it into the
final output — Word, PDF, or a webpage. Two separate steps, and when something
goes wrong it is useful to know which of the two failed.

Around this core there are many extensions: bookdown to write books, blogdown to
create websites, learnr to create interactive exercises, and many more. The basic
syntax is the same for all of these applications, which is why we focus on the
syntax here rather than on any one extension.

## Slide 10 · The five steps

The workflow has six steps, and the middle ones form a loop.

First you create the document. Second you fix the major metadata in the header.
Then you enter the cycle: write text in markdown syntax, embed R code in chunks,
render your document — and back to writing. Finally you share your work.

The single most important thing on this slide is that steps three to five are a
loop. Beginners write forty lines and then render once, and then have no idea
which of the forty lines broke the document. Render early and render often.

## Slide 11 · 1. Creating the document

First create a new Quarto document, and choose a template if an adequate one
exists. In R Studio that is New, then Quarto document.

There are plenty of templates distributed as packages — for journals, for
presentations, for reports. For learning purposes it is best to start with a
blank document, so that you see every line that is there.

After creating the document it is best to save it immediately, and where you save
it matters: either in the subdirectory `R`, or in a separate top-level directory
called `quarto`. We come back to why this matters in part three.

## Slide 12 · 2. Specify the header

The header contains the meta data. It starts and ends with three dashes, and
everything between them is YAML.

Usually you should set at least title, author and date. The output arguments —
everything under `format` — are usually set later, once you know what you want
the document to look like.

Two things about YAML that cause endless trouble: indentation is meaningful, and
the nesting expresses scope. Here `toc: true` is indented under `html`, which
means it applies only when the document is rendered to html. Get the indentation
wrong and the option is silently ignored.

There is a nice overview over the major keywords in the Quarto docs; see the
further readings.

## Slide 13 · 3. Write the main text

Writing the main text is the easy part: just write as you would in any normal
text editor, and to format it follow the Markdown syntax.

One tip that saves beginners a lot of frustration: R Studio has a Visual editor,
which you reach with the Source/Visual switch at the top left. It shows you the
formatted result while you type, much like a word processor. The file on disk is
still plain markdown — nothing is hidden from you — but you see the headings and
lists rendered while you work.

## Slide 14 · 4. Embed R code in chunks

R code is written within chunks. The keyboard shortcut on a Mac is Command,
Option, i — learn it, you will use it constantly.

Each chunk starts with three backticks followed by r in curly braces, and ends
with three backticks. Within the chunk you write R code just as you already know
it.

You can refer to variables defined in previous chunks. In principle you can refer
to all objects defined previously in your session — and that is precisely the
trap. Your session may contain objects that the document does not create. Make
sure everything you use was defined in a chunk **above** the one you are working
on; otherwise the document works for you and fails for everybody else, including
future-you after a restart.

## Slide 15 · Chunk options

How the R code gets shown and executed in the final document is controlled via
the chunk options.

Traditionally they were added to the first line of the chunk, inside the curly
braces. The modern variant puts them on their own lines inside the chunk, each
prefixed by a hash and a pipe. This is more consistent with the rest of Quarto
syntax, it reads better when you have several options, and it is what you should
use.

The most important single option is `echo`. With echo true you see the code and
the result; with echo false you see only the result. For a report that other
people read, `echo: false` is usually what you want.

## Slide 16 · Finding and setting chunk options

How do you find out which options exist? You get suggestions when pressing the
Tab key inside the chunk, and when creating a new chunk the point-and-click
option menu is available via the little gear icon.

More important for real documents: you can set default options for all chunks in
the YAML header of the document under the keyword `execute`. Setting `warning:
false` and `echo: false` once at the top is much better than repeating them in
twenty chunks — and if you later change your mind, you change one line.

The full list of all chunk options is in the Quarto docs at the link at the
bottom.

## Slide 17 · 5. Render the document

Rendering should in fact be done regularly during step three — this is the loop
from earlier. Otherwise it is hard to identify the source of an error, because
any of the last fifty lines could be responsible.

The format is determined in the header under `format`, and rendering produces the
output file right next to your qmd file, together with a folder holding its
figures and dependencies.

On the left you see the output options annotated. Note again the nesting: what is
indented under `html` applies only to html output. The theme sets fonts and
general properties; the toc entries control the table of contents; and
number-sections activates the numbering of sections.

For a complete overview over the output options and the possible themes, check
the Quarto docs for the format you actually want.

## Slide 18 · What the output options do

To make the effect concrete: the same document, once with a minimal header and
once with the output options set.

The minimal version gives you title, author and date, and then simply the
headings. The second version gives you a table of contents at the top, numbered
sections, and a different visual theme.

Nothing in the body of the document changed between the two. That is the point of
separating content from presentation — and it is why you should not spend time
formatting headings by hand.

## Slide 19 · 6. Share your work

There are many different possibilities for sharing your work, and the key
question is usually the format — a PDF travels by mail, a webpage needs a host.

Here we consider a very straightforward solution for html documents: Netlify
Drop. You literally drag the folder with your output into the browser window and
get a link back.

Three prerequisites. You create an html document. All relevant output data is in
one folder — that includes the figures folder, not only the html file. And your
output file must be called `index.html`, because that is the name a web server
looks for by default.

If you register with Netlify you can also choose a custom URL and keep the site
around; without registering the link still works, it is just anonymous.

## Slide 20 · Practice!

Now write and render a document yourself. The text should include a heading of
level one and of level two, a text body, and a plot made with ggplot2 — the code
for the plot is on the slide, so you can concentrate on the document rather than
on the plotting.

Also add meta data on author, title and date, render the document into html, and
deploy it via Netlify Drop, posting the link on Moodle.

Remember the naming requirement: the html file must be called index.html, so
either name your qmd file `index.qmd` or rename the output afterwards.

## Slide 22 · Remarks on project organisation

This is the part that catches nearly everybody at least once.

When rendering a qmd document, your computer is not using your current working
directory. Rather, the working directory is set to the location of the qmd file
itself. So if your qmd lives in the folder `R` and your data in `data/raw`, then
a relative path that worked perfectly in a script — `data/raw/file.csv` — is now
wrong, because it is interpreted relative to `R`.

This means you cannot simply copy-paste code containing relative paths from your
R scripts into a Quarto document, except if you use the `here` package. With
`here::here("data", "raw", "file.csv")` the anchor is the project root in both
cases, and the code moves between script and document unchanged.

So: `here::i_am()` at the top, and put your qmd files either into the folder `R`
or into a separate top-level directory called `quarto`.

## Slide 24 · Look at the rendered version

There are some very common mistakes. They screw up your document considerably and
make it painful to read — but they are actually very easy to avoid.

So after completing a markdown document, always look at the rendered version.
Check whether any of the problems on the next slide still exists and eliminate
them where necessary. Reading your own rendered document once, as a reader rather
than as an author, catches almost all of them.

As a task, download `DesasterMarkdown.pdf` from the course homepage and collect
the aspects that bother you the most. Then compare with the list on the next
slide — the overlap is usually large.

## Slide 25 · The black list of markdown turpitudes

The black list, and note that every single solution is a chunk option you already
know.

Overly long or wide tables: only print what is necessary, and check whether
`str()` or `dplyr::glimpse()` give a more adequate summary than printing the
whole data frame.

Uninformative warnings or messages: use the chunk options `warning` and
`message`, and consider setting the default to false in the header.

Too many or too few code chunks visible, and important output missing: both come
down to using `echo` and `include` correctly. Note that they are different —
`echo` controls whether the code is shown, `include` controls whether anything
from the chunk appears at all.

Figures in inappropriate sizes: adjust out-width and out-height, or fig-width and
fig-height.

And one upgrade worth knowing: `knitr::kable()` together with `kableExtra` turns
raw R output into a properly typeset table.

## Slide 26 · Summary and outlook

To summarise: Quarto allows you to write documents that contain R code to perform
statistical analysis and Markdown code to create formatted text using a plain
text editor.

This allows you to do and describe your statistical analysis within one
consistent document, which makes research fully transparent and reproducible —
the figure in your report cannot get out of sync with the data it came from,
because it is regenerated every time you render.

We covered the main steps of working with Quarto: create the document, set the
meta data in the header, write text, embed R code, render the document, and share
the final result. To learn markdown itself, just do the interactive tutorial.

And remember the last line: there are a few mistakes that might easily screw up
your document, but they are just as easy to avoid.
